report search limits instead of assuming every workflow reaches the function.

touched by the task diff or its changed data flow, inspect the task tree to
determine whether the defect persists.

do not let a focused task diff silently imply that inherited code can return
or otherwise operate successfully.

parent trees to find the code that reads the data back. Compare the writer's
and reader's resolved locations, inspect which parent directories are created,
and leave unexecuted filesystem-library behavior explicitly unestablished.

modules and package initializers that import the affected module, then state
how far an import-time failure reaches. If the explanation depends on a
language or library version fact, cite eligible documentation supplied in the
evidence catalog or state that the version fact is unestablished.

parent tree for the exact key and plausible near spellings. Inspect the task
diff and relevant consumers before describing the key's effect; do not infer
the intended spelling from the helper or variable name alone.
When a change makes a dictionary key or function argument required, search the
whole parent tree, including tests and utilities, for every builder of that
dictionary and every caller of the function. Inspect each relevant construction
site; a search limited to the implementation package cannot establish caller
compatibility.
When a documentation change describes command-line options, defaults or runtime
behavior, check every documented statement against the parser and relevant
consumers, not only statements that initially appear suspicious. Record loose
or unsupported claims and distinguish source inspection from execution.
When the commit message names a platform, product or error, search the whole
parent tree for that term before concluding that no in-scope source bears on it.
Report related occurrences without assuming they describe the same defect.
Do not infer author intent from later knowledge. Do not claim tests were run unless
a run result supports the claim. This is an authoring-boundary candidate, not a
request to publish or mark an entry reviewed.

Label every link you draw to the task as inference and state the concrete matching basis, such as a traceback line matching a source line.

Report what their own limits, tiers or preconditions show, as source inspection. State a conclusion about the author's reason as inference, and say that the rationale is unestablished only after that inspection.

Adds or changes means the task diff registers that architecture or modifies its model or configuration class. This applies to configuration files only; read tensor headers as needed to support claims.

These are navigation hints, not established relationships; fetch bodies with web_fetch, page with evidence_index(index_id="closed_discussions"), label task links as inference with their concrete basis, and report each item’s own title and framing faithfully.

find that commit's entry with the ancestor tools and read it before finalizing. Say which entries you read and
what they establish about the code the task relies on, including any guard, precondition or recorded defect; if
you read none, say so.

When one commit makes several edits, check whether any of them supplies a precondition another needs before
describing them as independent.

When the task starts calling an existing function, method or mechanism from a place that did not call it before,

the new call omits and state what the inspected code would do without it. If there are no other callers, say so.

When the task removes, comments out or bypasses a check, guard, conversion or initialisation, or replaces a call
that performed one, read the removed or bypassed code and say what it prevented or guaranteed. Then say whether
anything in the inspected code still prevents or guarantees it. If nothing does and the source shows an input or
call path that reaches the unguarded case, report it under findings as suspected, with its limits; do not leave
it only under uncertainty. If you could not establish a path that reaches it, say what you searched.

When the task adds or changes a model architecture, or code that names checkpoint tensors or depends on their

headers of at least one reference checkpoint for each distinct configuration. Say which tensor names and shapes
the changed code relies on and whether each exists with that shape, and name any stored tensors the code never
reads. Check every tensor name the code requests, including alternate and optional names, against the names in
the header, and say which are absent and which path the code then takes. Do not describe tensor layout as
unestablished while headers are available and unread.

import os

    from torch import version as torch_version

extension_name = "exllamav3_ext"
precompile = "EXLLAMA_NOCOMPILE" not in os.environ
verbose = "EXLLAMA_VERBOSE" in os.environ
ext_debug = "EXLLAMA_EXT_DEBUG" in os.environ

if precompile and not torch:
    print("Cannot precompile unless torch is installed.")
    print("To explicitly JIT install run EXLLAMA_NOCOMPILE= pip install <xyz>")

windows = os.name == "nt"

extra_cflags = ["/Ox"] if windows else ["-O3"]

if ext_debug:
    extra_cflags += ["-ftime-report", "-DTORCH_USE_CUDA_DSA"]

extra_cuda_cflags = ["-lineinfo", "-O3"]

if torch and torch_version.hip:
    extra_cuda_cflags += ["-DHIPBLAS_USE_HIP_HALF"]

extra_compile_args = {
    "cxx": extra_cflags,
    "nvcc": extra_cuda_cflags,
}

library_dir = "exllamav3"
sources_dir = os.path.join(library_dir, extension_name)
sources = [
    os.path.relpath(os.path.join(root, file), start=os.path.dirname(__file__))
    for root, _, files in os.walk(sources_dir)
    for file in files
    if file.endswith(('.c', '.cpp', '.cu'))
]

print (sources)

setup_kwargs = (
    {
        "ext_modules": [
            cpp_extension.CUDAExtension(
                extension_name,
                sources,
                extra_compile_args=extra_compile_args,
                libraries=["cublas"] if windows else [],
            )
        ],
        "cmdclass": {"build_ext": cpp_extension.BuildExtension},
    }
    if precompile and torch
    else {}
)

version_py = {}
with open("exllamav3/version.py", encoding="utf8") as fp:
    exec(fp.read(), version_py)
version = version_py["__version__"]
print("Version:", version)

setup(
    name="exllamav3",
    version=version,
    packages=[
        "exllamav3",
        "exllamav3.generator",
        "exllamav3.generator.sampler",
        "exllamav3.conversion",
        "exllamav3.models",
        "exllamav3.modules",
        "exllamav3.modules.quant",
        "exllamav3.modules.quant.exl3_lib",
        "exllamav3.tokenizer",
        "exllamav3.cache",
        "exllamav3.loader",
        "exllamav3.util",
    ],
    url="https://github.com/turboderp/exllamav3",
    license="MIT",
    author="turboderp",
    install_requires=[
        "torch>=2.6.0",
        "flash_attn==2.7.4.post1",
        "tokenizers>=0.21.1",
        "numpy>=2.1.0",
        "rich",
        "typing_extensions",
        "ninja",
        "safetensors>=0.3.2",
        "pyyaml",
        "marisa_trie",
        "kbnf>=0.4.2",
        "formatron>=0.5.0"
    ],
    include_package_data=True,
    package_data = {
        "": ["py.typed"],
    },
    verbose=verbose,
    **setup_kwargs,
)

      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "I'm also very wary of the compute requirement, but I did want to try this out so I gave it another go. Eventually, I was able to get it running alongside the other libraries I need. Had to jump through a lot of hoops, and apparently fast-hadamard-transform really doesn't like my 5090, but I ended up not needing it for the tests anyway.\n\n![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/66d94930-b32e-4c23-8d24-89baff8b3fe6)\n\nApparently the hybrid codebook does quite a bit better than the procedural ones at 2 bpw. Either that, or the blockwise regularization is at fault, though in a way that only manifests at 2 bpw for some reason. Might be worth revisiting both of those.\n\nFor YAQA there's only Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct to compare to, but the improvement is clear up to 3 bpw:\n\n![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6a06e588-3710-4479-ae70-40a79856990a)\n\nWish there were some more models to try out to see how well this holds across architectures and training recipes.",

    },
    {
      "author_login": "tsengalb99",
      "content": "Both of these results seem a bit odd to me. HYB should do worse than 3INST in general and I would have expected a larger KL gap in your testing, even at 4 bits. Is there documentation on where EXL3 differs from QTIP?",
      "content_sha256": "57827912c79f39ff65977b9a0bf7b1e5119c178295c52bdac06339e97442f23a",
      "created_at": "2025-06-07T20:00:06Z",

      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/49#issuecomment-2952951425"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "Sadly it's not really documented anywhere outside of the source code, and I'm also constantly tweaking it. I don't really have the bandwidth to thoroughly document everything I'm doing.\n\nAt its core, though, it's the same method as QTIP, or at least an attempt at an implementation of it. It's not inconceivable that something has been lost in translation, that there's some bad math somewhere, or maybe I'm rounding an intermediate value to float16 somewhere it really needs to be float32, or something. But outside of those possiblities, the main differences between EXL3 and QTIP/HYB are:\n\n1. Rather than a sample of RedPajama, The calibration dataset is a mix of English and multilingual data, and about 15% are random tokens to help discourage overfitting.\n\n2. Instead of rotating whole rows and columns, EXL3 rotates groups of 128 weights on either axis. This helps with kernel fusion, and more importantly it creates quantized tensors that can be split at load time to a granularity of 128 rows or columns, which lines up well with the head dimension of most models. So there's no need to requantize the same model for different tensor-parallel setups.\n\n    After this rotation, you end up with blocks of 128x128 weights that are individually close to being Gaussian, though obviously not to as high a degree as with whole-tensor regularization. They also have a greater number of outliers getting clamped during quantization. More alarmingly, these groups currently are not individually scaled, so there's an assumption that the RMS is roughly even between blocks, which is only like 95% sound.\n\n3. As for the other 5% (and to address a few especially difficult models), EXL3 also scales the input and output channels of each tensor individually, baking those scales into the su/sv tensors. This isn't foolproof, of course, and it was a bit of a kludge because I didn't want to revisit the GEMM kernel at the time to add block scales. But I'm working on those now, and then most likely the channel scales won't be needed. Early results suggest a somewhat smaller gap at 2 bpw this way.\n\n4. Before doing the final encoding on each tensor, the quantizer runs some test passes (without LDLQ) on a sample of 16x16 tiles along a wrapped diagonal to determine a fudge factor for the whole tensor. At higher bitrates (>2), at least with the implementation as it is, quantization definitely benefits from scaling down the input slightly below the RMS of the codebook. I haven't had time to fully explore this yet, but it makes sense that the penalty for doing so is lower at higher bitrates, while the penalty for outliers wholly outside the range of the codebook is constant, so there would be a happy medium somewhere for any given bitrate.\n\nAt any rate, I for sure haven't fully explored all of this. I felt that outperforming AQLM was a decent point at which to set quantization aside for a while and start focusing on other aspects of the library. But obviously I'm missing out on some of the potential of QTIP here.\n\nIt would be nice to have some models besides Llama to compare against. Are there by chance any other models you've already quantized while developing QTIP that are fit to release, just to have some more points of comparison? Both Mistral and Qwen2 should be compatible but have different training recipes.",
